title: SRE documentation: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE documentation standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single reference for on-call engineers, service owners, and platform teams responsible for production inference reliability.

Goals

- Provide a consistent SLO / error budget framework across inference services.
- Standardize capacity planning assumptions and processes for GPU and CPU-backed workloads.
- Define measurable reliability initiatives (quarterly) aligned with product priorities.
- Set incident review standards that produce actionable RCA and follow-ups.
- Describe required operational tooling, dashboards, and alerting minimal set.
- Provide canonical runbooks for common on-call scenarios and a runbook maintenance process.

1) SLO & SLI standards

Introduction
All public-facing and internal services that affect customer-facing inference must have at least one SLO. SLOs are expressed in terms of SLI measurements (availability, latency, correctness) and a target over an evaluation window.

Required SLI types (ordered by priority):
- Availability (success rate): 2xx responses for REST endpoints; successful completion for async jobs.
- Latency (p50/p95/p99): request-to-first-byte (TTFB) and request-to-last-byte for generation endpoints.
- Quality (model-level correctness): sample-based quality check tied to a golden prompt-set where applicable.

SLO template (must be included in each service's SLO doc):
- Service name: e.g., model-serving-api
- SLI(s): e.g., request_success_rate, p95_latency_ms
- SLO target: e.g., 99.9% success over 30d, p95 <= 250ms over 30d
- Measurement window: rolling 30d (default), quarterly for long-term strategic metrics
- Owner: team and PagerDuty escalation policy
- Measurement source: metrics (Grafana/Prometheus), tracing (Jaeger), and log-based fallback

Example SLOs (canonical):
| Service | SLI | SLO target | Window | Owner | Measurement source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| model-serving-api | request_success_rate | 99.95% | 30d | eng-serving-runtime | prometheus (http_requests_total, status_code) |
| model-serving-api (generation) | p95 latency (ms) | <= 350ms | 30d | eng-serving-runtime | tracing + prometheus histogram |
| embedding-service | request_success_rate | 99.99% | 30d | eng-platform | prometheus |

SLO calculation notes:
- Exclude planned maintenance windows and customer-approved private-deploy maintenance (apply scheduled_exclusion label).
- Use consistent sampling logic: 1-min bucket aggregation minimum.
- Quality SLOs should be tied to a test harness and run daily against a representative prompt set (see applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).

2) Error budget policy and automation

Definitions
- Error budget = 1 - SLO (for the evaluation window). For a 99.9% SLO over 30d, monthly error budget = 0.1% of requests in 30d.

Burn rate policy (operational):
- Normal: burn_rate < 2x -> track and notify service owner.
- Elevated: 2x <= burn_rate < 4x -> page on-call, require immediate mitigation plan within 60 minutes.
- Critical: burn_rate >= 4x or projected full budget burn within 24h -> page escalation (SEV process), pause non-critical deploys, disable risky feature flags, enable automated fallback model routes.

Automations tied to error-budget states:
- When elevated: create a ticket in the SRE tracker template, annotate with current burn-rate, owner, and mitigation steps.
- When critical: trigger a CI/CD hold: merge gates that allow production deploys will be blocked (bot posts explanation).
- Automated rollback: allowed only if telemetry indicates deploy correlation and owner approval not present within 30 minutes.

Communication and governance
- Weekly error budget review: every service with >10% exhausted budget must present a short runbook for mitigation and next steps.
- Quarterly reliability review: teams must document how error budgets affected release cadence and investment decisions.

3) Capacity planning: GPU, CPU, and networking

Forecasting and inputs
- Inputs: historical request volume (tokens/sec), average tokens per request, model selection mix, peak-to-average ratio, feature rollout plans, sales/marketing events.
- Forecast horizon: 90 days for tactical capacity; 12 months for strategic procurement/commitments.

Capacity guardrails and safety margins
- Production headroom: maintain minimum 30% spare throughput capacity per region for hosted services (reduces to 20% for dedicated reserved customers if contract specifies).
- Scaling unit: define a capacity unit (e.g., one nvidia-a100-80GB serving X tokens/sec for model family Y at quantized performance). Publish a per-model capacity table in eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling.

Procedure (90-day tactical capacity runbook):
1. Weekly metric pull: collect 30-day rolling peak, 99th percentile daily peak, and concurrency patterns.
2. Run model mix simulation: convert request mix into token throughput using current per-model perf profile.
3. Map throughput to instance types and autoscale groups.
4. Validate: run a staged traffic replay to a canary pool for predicted peak.
5. Purchase/allocate: request additional nodes (on cloud) or schedule provisioning (on-prem) with 14-day lead where applicable.

Burst and emergency capacity
- Burst policies: pre-configured burst pools (hot spare dedicated nodes) that auto-start for 15-120 minutes; usage must be reconciled and billed to feature owners.
- Emergency steps: if capacity exhausted and bursting insufficient, initiate cross-region fallback and model fallbacks (lower-cost variants/quantized models) with automated routing.

4) Reliability initiatives and roadmap alignment

Quarterly Reliability Initiative (R1) template (required):
- Initiative name
- Objective & measurable success criteria (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 20% for generation on 8k context models over Q1)
- Owner(s) and collaborators
- Start/End dates
- Key results (metrics + target)
- Runbook for rollout and rollback

Examples of typical initiatives:
- Continuous KV-cache improvements to reduce cold-start latency by 30%.
- Kernel selection automation to improve throughput for quantized LLM families by 2x.
- Observability expansion: add end-to-end tracing for private deployments.

Prioritization and investment
- Reliability initiatives are prioritized by expected user impact (SLO improvement) and cost savings (reduced token/infra cost). Product and SRE must approve cross-functional initiatives during the roadmap triage meeting.

5) Incident review standards (postmortem and RCA)

When to do a review
- All SEV1/SEV2 incidents affecting customer-facing SLOs require a postmortem within 72 hours (initial timeline) and a final RCA within 7 calendar days.
- SEV3 incidents: review required if error budget impact > 5% for the evaluation window or repeated occurrences.

Postmortem structure (required headings):
- Title and incident ID
- Summary (short blameless overview of what happened)
- Timeline (UTC timestamps, actions, state changes)
- Impact (customers affected, duration, SLO/error-budget impact)
- Root cause(s) analysis (why each contributing factor existed)
- Corrective actions (what will be done and owners with due dates)
- Preventative actions / follow-ups (tests, tooling, and automation)
- Lessons learned

RCA guidelines
- Use 5-whys at minimum to avoid superficial root causes.
- Distinguish between contributing causes and root causes.
- Each corrective action must have a clear owner and completion date; owners are auto-notified by the SRE tracker when due dates are approaching.

Blameless culture and review cadence
- Postmortems are blameless by default. Language that assigns personal fault is removed in final drafts.
- Monthly incident review meeting: review high-impact incidents and progress on long-running corrective actions.

6) Operational tooling: dashboards, alerts, runbook integrations

Minimal dashboards (per service)
- SLO dashboard: SLI, error budget burn rate, historical and rolling window.
- Request health: success rate, 4xx/5xx breakdown, and top error messages.
- Latency heatmap: p50/p95/p99 across model families and context lengths.
- Capacity dashboard: instance utilization, queued requests, GPU memory pressure, token throughput.

Alerting minimums
- SLI alert: if rolling 30d projected error budget burn exceeds 50% in next 24h -> notify owner and on-call.
- Latency alert: p95 crossing threshold for 10 minutes -> page on-call.
- Capacity alert: any GPU memory pressure > 85% for 5 minutes or node CPU > 90% for 5 minutes -> page infra on-call.
- Deployment correlation: deployments that change service version and are followed by spike in errors -> create auto-ticket and attach traces.

Runbook integration and automation
- Alerts must link directly to the canonical runbook for the symptom (link embedded in alert payload).
- Runbooks are stored in this Confluence space and referenced in a single-file index maintained by eng-sre/runbooks-index.
- Where possible, include one-click remediation actions (Grafana panel actions or orchestration playbook) with RBAC and audit logging.

7) Canonical runbook examples

Runbook: model-serving-api high p95 latency
- Symptom: sustained p95 latency > 350ms for 10 minutes or p99 > 1s.
- Immediate checks (first 10 minutes):
  1. Check SLO dashboard and error budget burn-rate.
  2. Verify recent deploys: git tag / ci job id. Command: curl -s https://ci.redwood.internal/api/latest-deploy?service=model-serving-api | jq
  3. Check instance autoscale groups and node counts in cloud console or with CLI: aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names <asg>
  4. Inspect GPU pressure: kubectl top pod -n inference | grep model-serving-api
  5. Look for request spikes: prometheus query for rate(http_requests_total[5m]) by model_family
- Mitigation steps (10-60 minutes):
  a. If deploy correlated: rollback to previous release (CI rollback playbook).
  b. If capacity correlated: scale out node pool by +2 units (automated script) and monitor.
  c. If model hot-spot: enable model fallback route to quantized variant (feature flag: model_fallback).
- Escalation (if unresolved after 60 minutes):
  - Page engineering lead and SRE on-call.
  - Consider cross-region failover and opening SEV process.
- Follow-up: create postmortem, record exact timestamps, attach traces, and schedule corrective actions.

Runbook: 5xx error spike from the generation service
- Symptom: sudden increase in 5xx rate > 0.5% of traffic sustained for 5 minutes.
- Immediate checks:
  1. Check logs for top error signatures (search Es index: errors-YYYY.MM.DD).
  2. Confirm any third-party dependency outages (KMS, object store, internal auth).
  3. Verify DB or config store latencies (etcd, redis).
- Mitigations:
  - If dependency down: enable graceful degradation (serve cached responses or return degraded response with 200 + warning header).
  - If config corruption: revert recent config change and redeploy.

Runbook lifecycle and maintenance
- Ownership: each runbook must list an owner and a last_reviewed date.
- Review cadence: runbooks must be reviewed at least quarterly or after any SEV incident that used that runbook.
- Test drills: schedule at least one game-day per quarter to exercise high-severity runbooks and verify automation paths.

8) Ownership, training, and onboarding

- On-call training: all new on-call members must complete the SRE on-call bootcamp (2-day) and a recorded runbook walkthrough.
- Runbook ownership: team leads must nominate runbook owners and backup owners.
- Knowledge transfer: postmortem corrective actions that require code changes must include a short recorded demo for the platform team.

9) Templates and artifacts

- SLO definition template (copy and paste into service page)
- Postmortem template (link and checklist)
- Capacity planning worksheet (spreadsheet with model perf profiles)
- Runbook checklist (owner, last_reviewed, test_instructions, CLI commands)

Appendix: example SLO definition (copy)
Service name: model-serving-api
SLI(s): request_success_rate, p95_latency_ms
SLO target: request_success_rate >= 99.95% over 30d; p95_latency_ms <= 350ms over 30d
Measurement: prometheus (http_requests_total, http_request_duration_seconds histogram); trace sampling 10%
Exclusions: scheduled_maintenance label; private-deployments with customer-approved maintenance windows
Owner: eng-serving-runtime, pager: eng-serving-runtime-oncall@pagerduty

If you have questions or need new templates added, contact eng-sre slack (#eng-sre) or the doc owner.
